name: Savings bank account
oneLiner: A bank deposit account that pays a low rate of interest and allows withdrawal on demand; it is the liquidity layer of a portfolio, not an investment.
returnMechanism: The bank pays a contractual interest rate on the daily balance, set by the bank itself within RBI rules and historically linked to the repo rate after the 2019 deregulation. The return is entirely interest; there is no market participation. Banks pay materially less than they earn on the same money, so the spread is the bank's, not the depositor's.
expectedReturn: Contractually small, set by each bank and typically the lowest rate in the deposit ladder. No upside beyond the advertised rate.
historicalReturnNote: Savings rates have moved with the rate cycle but have generally trailed fixed-deposit rates and inflation over long periods; real returns have often been negative or close to zero.
maxDrawdownNote: The rupee balance does not fall, but the real purchasing power of the balance erodes with inflation.
minimumInvestment: Account-opening minimums are bank-specific and small
taxTreatment: Interest is taxed at slab rates as income from other sources. A limited deduction for savings-account interest exists only under the old regime; tax is deducted at source only above the statutory threshold and the threshold differs for senior citizens.
fees: No explicit charge to hold a balance, but minimum-balance penalties, cash-handling charges above free limits and debit-card fees are real costs. The economic cost is mostly the opportunity cost of the low rate.
investorEligibility: Any resident individual, HUF, firm or company that meets the bank's KYC requirements; NRIs can hold accounts with specific non-resident designations.
risks: Real return is often negative after inflation
Deposit insurance covers each depositor per bank only up to a statutory ceiling that has changed over time
Minimum-balance penalties silently reduce the effective return
Co-operative banks and small institutions have different risk and insurance positions than scheduled commercial banks
suitability: Appropriate for transaction balances, emergency-fund parking and money needed within weeks. Not a place for long-term savings or for money you will not touch for years.
commonMistakes: Treating the savings balance as an emergency fund without checking it covers several months of expenses
Leaving large idle balances in savings when a sweep-in or liquid fund would earn more with the same same-day access
Assuming the balance is fully insured beyond the statutory deposit-insurance ceiling

name: Sweep-in fixed deposit
oneLiner: A savings account linked to a fixed deposit that automatically advances or returns money as the balance crosses a threshold, paying FD rates on the swept portion while keeping same-day access.
returnMechanism: The bank maintains the account balance at an agreed floor and sweeps the excess into a linked fixed deposit that earns the bank's FD card rate. When spending needs exceed the balance, the bank breaks the deposit in a defined order. The return is contractual interest, higher than pure savings interest but usually below a separately locked FD of the same tenor.
expectedReturn: Close to the bank's short-tenor fixed-deposit rate on the swept balance, with the convenience of same-day access; the rate is reset by the bank and is not a market return.
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific threshold above which balances are swept
taxTreatment: Interest is taxed at slab rates as income from other sources, reported by the bank even if the deposit has not been broken. TDS applies above the threshold.
fees: Usually no explicit fee, but some banks charge for premature withdrawal of the swept deposit or pay a lower penalty rate on the broken portion.
investorEligibility: Any account holder the bank accepts; the feature is bank-specific and must be enabled.
risks: Swept deposits can be broken in an order the depositor did not intend, potentially breaking the longest-tenor deposit first
The effective rate is bank-specific and lower than a directly negotiated FD
Interest on the swept portion is taxable even before it is realised in cash
Not all banks offer the same sweep mechanics; the terms are in the account mandate
suitability: Useful for a contingency reserve that must be accessible the same day but should not earn zero. Not a substitute for a term-locked FD ladder or for long-term goals.
commonMistakes: Assuming sweep balances are covered by the same protections as a manually created deposit without reading the mandate
Keeping the sweep for money that is actually a long-term goal and would earn more in a tenor-matched instrument
Forgetting that swiped interest is taxable each year

name: Retail bank fixed deposit
oneLiner: A lump-sum deposit with a scheduled commercial bank for a fixed term at a contracted rate, with a regulated deposit guarantee up to a statutory ceiling.
returnMechanism: The bank pays a contracted interest rate for the stated term because it uses the deposit to fund lending and investments. The return is entirely contractual interest; there is no equity or market upside. The real return depends on whether the nominal rate exceeds inflation and tax.
expectedReturn: Contractually set at the bank's published card rate for the chosen tenor; card rates are reset by the bank from time to time and senior citizens are usually offered a small premium. No equity upside.
historicalReturnNote: FD rates have moved with the policy rate cycle; over long periods, pre-tax FD returns have roughly tracked inflation while post-tax real returns have often been low or negative for higher-slab investors.
maxDrawdownNote: The rupee value of a deposit does not fall with markets. Premature withdrawal incurs a penalty rate cut, and inflation erodes real value.
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is fully taxable at slab rates, accruing each year even on cumulative deposits where no cash is received. TDS applies above the statutory threshold, which is higher for senior citizens, and a limited deduction for deposit interest exists only under the old regime.
fees: No entry fee; premature withdrawal usually reduces the applicable rate by a penalty margin. Interest is often paid quarterly or reinvested, which changes the effective yield.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals, HUFs, firms and companies; NRIs can hold NRO and NRE deposits with specific rules on repatriation and interest.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Bank card rates change over time and vary by bank and tenor; replace with the rate actually offered to you.

risks: Real return can be negative after tax and inflation
Deposit insurance covers each depositor per bank only up to the statutory ceiling, which has changed over time
Reinvestment risk: the rate available at maturity may be lower
Laddering and endurance risk: locking a long tenor forecloses better rates later
suitability: The backbone of a conservative rupee allocation and goal-based pots where the date and amount are known. Not suitable as the growth engine of a long-horizon portfolio.
commonMistakes: Comparing the headline rate without computing the post-tax real return
Ignoring the annual accrual tax on cumulative deposits
Spreading deposits across banks without checking which institutions fall within the insurance net
Renewing automatically at whatever rate the bank offers on maturity

name: Tax-saving fixed deposit
oneLiner: A bank fixed deposit with a mandated minimum lock-in that qualifies for a deduction on contribution under the old tax regime.
returnMechanism: The return is ordinary deposit interest, identical in kind to a normal fixed deposit. The economic difference is not in where the money comes from but in the lock-in and the deduction, which improves the post-tax outcome only for an investor who can actually use the deduction under the old regime.
expectedReturn: Contractually set at the bank's card rate for the mandated tenor; usually no senior-citizen premium difference from the bank's standard card. No upside.
lockIn: A minimum lock-in mandated by the tax provision (few years); no premature withdrawal is permitted during the lock-in
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is fully taxable at slab rates and is not exempted by the lock-in. The deduction on contribution is available only under the old regime and is subject to the overall ceiling on such deductions, so the product's tax benefit disappears under the default new regime.
fees: No explicit fee; the economic cost of the lock-in is the inability to switch if rates rise.
investorEligibility: Available to individuals and HUFs that can claim the deduction under the old regime; the lock-in applies to the depositor.
risks: The tax deduction is unusable under the default new regime, leaving only a locked low-yield deposit
Lock-in prevents switching when rates rise
Interest is taxable, so the post-tax return is materially lower than the headline rate for higher-slab investors
Opportunity cost against ELSS or NPS for the same deduction
suitability: Only for an investor who has chosen the old regime, genuinely needs the deduction, and wants no market risk. For anyone else, a plain FD plus a separate equity allocation usually dominates.
commonMistakes: Assuming the interest is tax-free because the deposit is tax-saving
Buying it without confirming the deduction is usable in the chosen regime
Treating the deduction as a return rather than as a reduction in tax

name: Corporate fixed deposit
oneLiner: A deposit placed with a non-bank company, typically an NBFC or housing finance company, which pays a higher rate than a bank FD because the depositor takes unsecured corporate risk.
returnMechanism: The company pays a contracted rate for the use of the money in its lending or operating business. The extra yield over a bank deposit is compensation for the absence of bank-grade regulation and deposit protection, not a free premium. If the issuer defaults, recovery depends on the unsecured claim.
expectedReturn: Contractually set by the issuer in its scheme; typically offered above bank card rates. Capped by the issuer's cost of funds, and the premium is the price of credit risk.
historicalReturnNote: Issuer failures have occurred across cycles in the corporate-deposit segment, with prolonged repayment delays for depositors.
maxDrawdownNote: The stated balance does not fluctuate, but a credit event can impair or delay principal and interest permanently, which is a real drawdown in economic terms.
lockIn: Scheme-specific fixed tenors, typically one to several years
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, usually small
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates in the year it accrues, with TDS above the applicable threshold. Interest on company deposits is not covered by the deposit-insurance scheme that covers banks.
fees: No entry cost; some issuers have agency commissions embedded in the scheme economics. Premature withdrawal terms are issuer-specific and can be punitive.
investorEligibility: Any investor the issuer accepts; companies raising public deposits are subject to regulatory conditions and rating requirements, but the terms are issuer-specific.
risks: Unsecured exposure to a single corporate borrower
Ratings and financial statements can deteriorate faster than a fixed-deposit holder can react
Repayment delays and one-sided renewal terms after maturity
Lack of deposit insurance; resolution can take years
suitability: Only for investors who can evaluate the issuer's credit standing and can hold to maturity without needing the money. Not a substitute for a bank FD in an emergency fund.
commonMistakes: Chasing the rate differential without reading the rating and the issuer's asset quality
Concentrating several deposits with one group
Assuming a high rating removes the risk rather than pricing it

name: Small finance bank fixed deposit
oneLiner: A fixed deposit with a small finance bank, which typically pays more than a large bank because its borrower base and funding profile are riskier.
returnMechanism: Interest is contractual, funded by the bank's lending to segments that mainstream banks serve less. The rate premium compensates the depositor for the bank's higher-risk loan book and, in some cases, weaker funding franchises.
expectedReturn: Contractually set by the bank; generally above the card rates of large private and public banks. No upside; the premium is a risk price.
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates; TDS thresholds apply as for other banks, with a higher threshold for senior citizens. Deposit insurance applies per depositor per bank up to the statutory ceiling, as with any insured bank.
fees: No entry fee; premature withdrawal penalty follows the bank's schedule.
investorEligibility: Any depositor the bank accepts, subject to its KYC and scheme terms; NRI eligibility differs across small finance banks.
risks: The rate premium reflects a riskier loan book
Deposit insurance caps the protected amount per depositor per bank
Some banks have concentrated exposure to unsecured microfinance or small-ticket lending
Access to branches and digital services can be thinner than at large banks
suitability: One rung of a deposit ladder for an investor who wants a higher contractual rate and can accept bank-level risk within the insurance ceiling. Not for concentrated large sums above the insurance cover unless the credit work is done.
commonMistakes: Depositing far above the insurance ceiling at one bank for the rate
Assuming all small finance banks carry the same risk
Ignoring the concentration of the bank's loan book

name: Co-operative bank fixed deposit
oneLiner: A fixed deposit with an urban or district co-operative bank, often offering attractive rates but with governance and resolution arrangements that differ from commercial banks.
returnMechanism: Contractual interest funded by the bank's local lending. The premium over large-bank rates reflects the co-operative sector's weaker capital positions, governance variability and thinner liquidity, and the fact that depositor recovery in a failure has historically been slow.
expectedReturn: Contractually set by the bank; frequently higher than commercial-bank card rates. The rate is a price for institutional risk.
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates with the same TDS framework as other banks, though payer classifications and thresholds can differ. Deposit insurance applies to co-operative banks within the scheme, but with the same per-depositor ceiling and with practical differences in the claims process.
fees: No entry fee; premature withdrawal penalties are set by the bank.
investorEligibility: Depositors the bank accepts, with membership conditions in some multi-state and state co-operative structures.
risks: Weaker published financial disclosure than commercial banks
Resolution of a failed co-operative bank has historically been slow, with restricted access to deposits
Concentration in local real estate and related lending
Governance risk in some institutions
suitability: Only with deliberate limits and diversification, and only where the depositor has reviewed the bank's published financials. Not a place for a large share of savings.
commonMistakes: Treating a co-operative bank as identical to a scheduled commercial bank
Concentrating more than the insurance ceiling at one institution
Being drawn by the highest local rate without reading the bank's financials

name: Bank recurring deposit
oneLiner: A monthly deposit commitment into a bank for a fixed term, with each instalment earning the applicable rate and the whole amount repaid at maturity.
returnMechanism: The bank pays contracted interest on each instalment for the time it remains deposited. Because instalments arrive monthly, the effective yield is below the headline rate on a lump sum held for the whole term; the quoted rate is applied to the reducing balance of the accumulated deposits.
expectedReturn: Contractually set by the bank's RD card rate; typically close to the FD rate of the same tenor, with the same absence of upside.
minimumInvestment: Bank-specific monthly instalment, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest accrues and is taxable at slab rates each year, and the accrued amount is reported by the bank even though no cash is received until maturity. TDS applies above the threshold.
fees: Penalties apply for missed instalments and for premature closure, typically a rate cut plus a charge.
investorEligibility: Any bank customer who can commit to the monthly schedule.
risks: Missed instalments attract penalties and can erode the effective yield
The annual accrual tax is payable before cash is received, creating a cash-flow mismatch for cumulative RDs
The effective yield on a monthly-instalment structure is lower than the headline RD rate quoted
Premature closure is penalised
suitability: A disciplined forced-saving vehicle for a fixed monthly surplus where market risk is unacceptable. For a long-horizon goal, a systematic plan into a market instrument usually has a better expected post-tax outcome.
commonMistakes: Comparing the RD rate with an FD rate without adjusting for the instalment schedule
Forgetting the annual interest accrual for tax
Stopping instalments mid-term and absorbing penalties

name: Post office time deposit
oneLiner: A fixed-term deposit sold at post offices with a sovereign-backed issuer and rates reset administratively, sitting between a bank FD and a small-savings certificate.
returnMechanism: The government pays a rate set by administrative formula and reviewed periodically. The return is contractual interest only; there is no market participation and no equity upside.
expectedReturn: Set administratively and reset periodically; observed rates have historically been broadly comparable to bank fixed-deposit rates for similar tenors, but any quoted rate is a point-in-time figure.
minimumInvestment: Scheme minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates; some tenors of small-savings deposits qualify for a deduction on contribution under the old regime, which the new regime does not provide. TDS applies above the statutory threshold.
fees: No entry fee; premature withdrawal is permitted only on the scheme's conditions and usually with a rate adjustment.
investorEligibility: Any eligible individual, including a minor through a guardian; NRIs are generally not permitted to open these accounts.
risks: Rates are reset administratively and can fall at renewal
Long tenors lock the money with only limited premature-exit options
Interest is fully taxable, so a high-slab investor's real return may be negative
Physical-account servicing is slower than digital bank servicing
suitability: For conservative savers who value the sovereign issuer and are comfortable with post-office servicing. It is a close substitute for a bank FD, not a growth asset.
commonMistakes: Assuming the scheme interest is tax-exempt
Ignoring that only some tenors qualify for the deduction under the old regime
Opening a long tenor and then needing the money early

name: Government of India dated securities (RBI Retail Direct)
oneLiner: Direct holdings of central government bonds bought by retail investors through the RBI Retail Direct facility, with sovereign credit risk and market-priced interest rate risk.
returnMechanism: The bond pays a contracted coupon on face value and repays principal at maturity. If held to maturity, the return is the coupon plus or minus the difference between purchase price and face value. If sold early, price moves with the market yield, creating capital gain or loss on top of accrued coupon.
expectedReturn: The coupon is set at auction and reflects the market yield curve at issue; a buyer in the secondary market earns the yield at which they buy, which changes daily. Yields are a market price, not a promised outcome.
historicalReturnNote: Government bonds have delivered the coupon plus rate-cycle capital gains and losses; long duration has produced large swings in total return even with sovereign credit.
maxDrawdownNote: Prices fall when yields rise; the fall is larger for longer-dated bonds. A holder to maturity avoids realising it but still bears opportunity cost if yields rise.
minimumInvestment: Retail Direct primary-auction minimums are small and set by the facility; verify current terms on the platform
taxTreatment: Coupon interest is taxable at slab rates as income from other sources. Gains on listed government securities held more than the applicable long-term threshold are long-term capital gains without indexation; gains on shorter holdings are short-term and taxed at slab. No securities transaction tax applies.
fees: No entry load; the facility charges no commission on primary auctions, while secondary purchases and sales involve spreads and platform charges. There is no fund expense ratio.
investorEligibility: Individual investors and specified non-individual entities with an RBI Retail Direct account and the required KYC; NRIs face separate eligibility conditions that must be verified.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Assume a mid-duration holding; the actual outcome depends on the yield at purchase and the rate path. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Interest rate risk: prices fall when yields rise, more so at longer maturities
Reinvestment risk: coupons received in a falling-rate environment earn less
Secondary-market liquidity is thinner for retail-sized quantities, so bid-ask spreads can be wide
Temptation to sell during a rate rally and then stay out
suitability: For investors who want sovereign credit risk with a known coupon and can hold to maturity or accept price swings. A natural building block for a liability-matched debt allocation; not a growth asset.
commonMistakes: Buying long-dated bonds for the coupon and being surprised by price falls
Assuming coupons are tax-free
Confusing yield to maturity with the coupon rate
Ignoring the reinvestment assumption embedded in a YTM figure

name: Treasury bill
oneLiner: A short-dated central government instrument (up to one year) sold at a discount to face value and redeemed at par, used for near-cash sovereign parking.
returnMechanism: The investor pays less than face value today and receives face value at maturity; the difference is the return, which is economically interest. If sold before maturity, the realised price depends on the short-rate market at that time.
expectedReturn: Yield at issue is set by auction and tracks the very short end of the sovereign curve, so it moves with policy rates. The return is a discount accretion, not a coupon.
minimumInvestment: Primary-market minimums are set by the auction facility; verify current terms
taxTreatment: Held to maturity, the discount is treated as interest income taxable at slab rates. A sale before maturity produces a capital gain computed on the price difference; because these are not securities transaction tax-paid listed equities, no concessional equity rate or exemption applies.
fees: No commission on primary auction participation through the retail facility; secondary spreads are small in normal markets.
investorEligibility: Investors eligible for the auction channel used (retail facility or broker); eligibility conditions should be verified for the specific route.
risks: Returns are low and can be below inflation
Interest income is taxable at slab, which can push the post-tax real return negative for higher earners
Reinvestment of a maturing bill must itself be managed
Auction access and settlement mechanics differ across platforms
suitability: A sovereign alternative to a liquid fund or short deposit for money that must be parked for weeks to months with no credit risk. Not a long-term savings vehicle.
commonMistakes: Treating the discount as a capital gain and ignoring its interest character
Comparing the annualised yield with a bank deposit without adjusting for tax timing
Using T-bills for money that needs instant access

name: State Development Loan
oneLiner: A dated bond issued by a state government, carrying the state's credit rather than the Union's, and usually yielding a small premium to central government bonds of similar tenor.
returnMechanism: The state pays a contracted coupon and repays at maturity; the small yield premium over central government bonds is the market's price for state-level credit and liquidity differences. Secondary-market prices move with the general yield curve.
expectedReturn: Coupon set at auction; yields typically sit slightly above central government bonds of comparable tenor. The spread is small and is not a free premium.
maxDrawdownNote: Prices move with interest rates; liquidity is thinner than central government bonds, so selling can involve a wider spread.
minimumInvestment: Auction minimums are set by the facility used; verify current terms
taxTreatment: Coupon is taxable at slab rates. Listed state loans benefit from the capital-gains framework for listed securities in the same way as central government securities; no securities transaction tax applies.
fees: No commission on primary auction participation through the retail facility; secondary trades carry a spread.
investorEligibility: Investors eligible for the facility used to buy; NRI conditions differ from those for central government securities and must be verified.
risks: State credit is not identical to Union credit even if no default has occurred on a state loan
Thin retail liquidity relative to central government bonds
Interest rate risk on longer tenors
Taxed coupon income at slab rates
suitability: A marginal yield pickup over central government bonds for an investor building a sovereign debt ladder. The premium is small, so it is not worth reaching for unless the tenor and liquidity suit the plan.
commonMistakes: Assuming state loans are automatically as liquid as central government bonds
Blaming price falls on the state's credit rather than the rate cycle
Holding to maturity without planning the reinvestment

name: Sovereign Gold Bond
oneLiner: A government security denominated in grams of gold that pays a small fixed interest and redeems at the prevailing gold price, removing custody cost but adding a long lock-up.
returnMechanism: The return has two parts: a small contractual interest on the issue value and the change in the gold reference price between issue and redemption. The interest is paid by the government; the gold exposure is synthetic, with no physical delivery outside specified windows.
expectedReturn: A small fixed interest plus gold price change; the interest rate is tranche-specific. Gold price change is not forecastable, so the total return is dominated by the gold leg.
historicalReturnNote: Gold has delivered strong discrete rallies and long flat periods; the bond's structure converts those moves into rupee outcomes without storage or making charges.
maxDrawdownNote: The bond price tracks gold and can fall meaningfully in rupee terms; the interest is fixed and does not offset a large gold drawdown.
lockIn: A long maturity fixed by tranche, with an early-exit window available only after a set number of years on interest payment dates
minimumInvestment: Tranche-specific small minimum in grams; verify the terms of the tranche
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates. Redemption by an individual at maturity is exempt from capital gains under the special provision for these bonds. A sale in the secondary market before maturity is treated differently and is not covered by that exemption, so the route matters. Whether new tranches are being issued is a time-sensitive question that must be verified.
fees: No annual custody or fund fee, which is the bond's main cost advantage over a gold ETF; secondary-market sales involve a spread, and the issue may have a small discount or premium.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals and specified entities subject to tranche terms and investment caps; joint holding and nomination rules are tranche-specific.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast; deliberately split between a small fixed interest and an assumed long-run gold price drift. Gold returns are not predictable. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Gold price falls and the fixed interest does not compensate
Long lock-up with early exit only in defined windows
New-issue availability is not permanent, and secondary-market pricing may be unfavourable
Redemption mechanics and tax treatment differ between maturity redemption and secondary-market sale
suitability: For a gold allocation in a taxable account where the investor wants no storage or fund cost and can accept the lock-up. Not a short-term trading vehicle, and less useful for an investor who may need the money before the exit window.
commonMistakes: Assuming the interest rate is a total return
Forgetting that a secondary-market sale does not get the maturity exemption
Buying near the end of the issue window without checking the redemption date
Assuming new tranches will always be available when needed

name: Public Provident Fund
oneLiner: A 15-year government savings account with an administratively set interest rate and exempt-exempt-exempt tax treatment, designed as long-horizon, no-market-risk savings.
returnMechanism: The government pays an interest rate reset periodically against a formula linked to government security yields. The return is entirely the administratively declared interest, compounded annually; there is no participation in any market and no equity upside.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically, so any quoted rate is a point-in-time figure. The mechanism links the rate loosely to sovereign yields; it is not a market return.
historicalReturnNote: Rates have been revised repeatedly and have trended down over long periods in line with the rate cycle; because interest is exempt, the post-tax comparison with taxable instruments is materially better than the headline rate suggests.
maxDrawdownNote: The balance never falls in nominal terms and interest is credited annually; the risk is a real-return decline if inflation and future rates diverge.
lockIn: 15 years from the year of opening, with permitted partial withdrawal conditions and extension in blocks after maturity
minimumInvestment: A small minimum annual deposit with a statutory maximum that is set administratively; deposits above the maximum earn no interest
taxTreatment: Exempt-exempt-exempt: contributions qualify for a deduction under the old regime only, interest accrues free of tax and the maturity balance is exempt in both regimes. Because the interest is exempt, its value rises with the investor's marginal rate.
fees: No expense ratio or entry cost; opening is through a bank or post office, and there is no intermediary commission of the kind a fund carries.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals, with the account opened in the investor's own name and limited additional accounts under the rules; non-residents are generally restricted to continuing an account opened while resident, subject to conditions.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. The rate is reset administratively; replace it with the currently notified rate in any model.

risks: Administrative rate resets can reduce future accrual
Long lock-up with limited partial access
A skipped year has a cost and can disrupt the account's continuity
Because interest is nominal and fixed, inflation can erode real value over 15 years
suitability: Core tax-free debt allocation for long-horizon goals, particularly for investors whose alternatives are taxable deposits. Not suitable for money needed in the medium term or as the growth engine of a portfolio.
commonMistakes: Withdrawing or closing early without understanding the rules and costs
Using a loan against PPF when a simpler option exists
Stopping deposits after a few years and losing the tax-free compounding
Not extending the account after maturity when it suits the plan

name: Employees' Provident Fund (employee account)
oneLiner: A mandatory retirement account for salaried employees, funded by monthly employee and employer contributions, paying an administratively determined interest rate with exempt treatment on satisfied withdrawals.
returnMechanism: The EPFO pays interest declared annually on the accumulated balance, funded by returns on its holdings of central and state government securities and other permitted instruments. The member's return is a declared rate, not the underlying portfolio return.
expectedReturn: An administratively declared rate announced each year; it is not a market rate and it is not guaranteed for future years. For a salaried employee, the employer's match makes the effective return higher than the declared rate alone.
lockIn: Continuous employment-linked; withdrawal before the continuity requirement attracts tax on the balance including the employer's share, subject to exceptions
taxTreatment: Contributions qualify for deduction under the old regime; the accumulated balance is exempt on completing the continuity condition, with exceptions for earlier cessation. Interest attributable to an employee's own high-balance contributions has been made partially taxable through an administrative mechanism, and the employer's contribution above the statutory limit can be a taxable perquisite. Premature withdrawal can attract TDS where it is taxable.
fees: No fund management charge of the kind a mutual fund carries; the EPFO's administrative cost is borne within the scheme. The economic cost is the rigidity of the account.
investorEligibility: Employees of establishments covered by the fund; the employee's contribution is a fixed percentage of wages, and the employer matches a portion as prescribed.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. The declared rate changes annually; replace with the currently announced rate in any model.

risks: Administrative rate changes reduce long-run accrual
Sharp withdrawal rules on job changes and premature exit
The employer's timely deposit of contributions cannot be assumed at every establishment
Concentration of a young worker's entire retirement saving in one administratively run account
suitability: A mandatory, low-cost, tax-advantaged core for salaried retirement saving; the employer's match makes participation rational for almost every employee. It should be complemented, not replaced, by market instruments for growth.
commonMistakes: Withdrawing on a job change instead of transferring the account
Assuming the declared rate is fixed or guaranteed
Ignoring that premature withdrawal can be taxed
Failing to keep service records for the continuity test

name: National Pension System (Tier 1)
oneLiner: A regulated, contribution-based pension account that invests in equity, corporate debt, government securities and alternative assets according to a chosen allocation, with a lock-up to retirement.
returnMechanism: The account holds market instruments, so the return comes from the earnings of those instruments: equity earnings growth and dividends, and interest on the debt sleeves. The pension fund manager's allocation determines most of the outcome, and the return is net of low capped charges.
expectedReturn: Driven by the chosen allocation: a high-equity active choice has a market-linked expected return with real short-term risk; a government-securities-heavy choice behaves like a bond portfolio. No rate is guaranteed.
historicalReturnNote: Pension fund schemes have produced market-linked returns across the choices over their history, with equity-heavy choices showing wider dispersion between good and bad periods.
maxDrawdownNote: Equity-heavy choices fall with markets; the long accumulation horizon and continued contributions are the designed mitigants.
lockIn: Locked to retirement age for the main corpus, with partial withdrawal permitted only for specified purposes and after a minimum contribution period
minimumInvestment: A small minimum per contribution and a minimum annual amount; Tier 1 and Tier 2 have different minimums
taxTreatment: Contributions can qualify for deduction subject to an overall ceiling, and an additional deduction is available within a separate limit under the old regime; an employer's contribution qualifies for deduction in both regimes, subject to limits, which is its distinctive tax advantage. At exit, the lump-sum share is exempt subject to conditions, and the annuitised portion is taxed at slab rates as annuity income is received.
fees: Among the lowest-cost retirement products: charge caps cover account opening, contribution processing, fund management and other service elements, and the fund management charge is a small fraction of a percentage of assets.
investorEligibility: Any individual citizen (resident or NRI) subject to the scheme's KYC; corporate NPS is available through an employer arrangement.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. The figure is a blended assumption; your outcome depends on the allocation choice you select. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Market risk in the equity and corporate-debt sleeves
The mandatory annuitisation at exit converts part of the corpus into a product with its own low real return
Exit in a high-income year is tax-inefficient because annuity income is taxed at slab
Allocation choices can be left at a default that is more conservative than intended
suitability: A low-cost, structurally sound retirement accumulator for a long-horizon saver who wants market-linked growth with a disciplined lock-up and a tax-advantaged employer contribution. Not a substitute for a liquid debt allocation or for an early-retirement corpus.
commonMistakes: Leaving the allocation on auto with no review for decades
Ignoring the annuitisation requirement when projecting retirement cash flows
Comparing NPS with a mutual fund without accounting for the exit tax structure
Choosing a fund manager purely on a short period of recent returns

name: Sukanya Samriddhi Account
oneLiner: A government savings account opened for a daughter with an administratively set rate and exempt-exempt-exempt treatment, with deposits for a fixed window and a longer maturity.
returnMechanism: The government pays a declared interest rate, reset periodically, compounded annually on the balance. The return is entirely administrative interest; there is no market participation and no equity upside.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically; any quoted rate is a point-in-time figure. The mechanism is the same as other small-savings schemes.
lockIn: Deposits permitted for a fixed number of years with maturity later still; partial withdrawal for education is permitted only on the scheme's conditions and after a minimum age
minimumInvestment: A small minimum annual deposit with a statutory maximum set administratively; deposits above the maximum earn no interest
taxTreatment: Contributions qualify for a deduction under the old regime only; interest and maturity proceeds are exempt where the scheme conditions are satisfied. The exemption does not depend on the regime choice.
fees: No entry cost or expense ratio; the economic cost is the illiquidity and the fixed deposit window.
investorEligibility: A parent or legal guardian may open an account for a daughter, subject to the scheme's limits on the number of accounts per family and exceptions stated in the rules.
risks: Rate resets over a long horizon
The long deposit and maturity structure means the last deposits have an effective duration longer than the deposit window
Partial withdrawal conditions are narrow
Inflation erodes the fixed nominal accrual
suitability: A disciplined, tax-exempt, no-market-risk pot for a daughter's future education or marriage, funded from surplus after the family's core goals are covered. Not a growth allocation.
commonMistakes: Assuming the account is unlimited when a statutory maximum annual deposit applies
Opening more accounts than the rules permit
Relying on partial withdrawal to fund general expenses
Forgetting to deposit in a year and losing interest on that year's balance

name: National Savings Certificate
oneLiner: A fixed-tenor post-office certificate that accrues interest instead of paying it, with the accrual treated as reinvested for the deduction framework under the old regime.
returnMechanism: The certificate accrues a declared rate for its fixed tenor and pays the compounded amount at maturity. The return is entirely administrative interest; nothing is linked to a market.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically; the accrued interest is reinvested within the certificate rather than paid out, so the maturity value compounds the declared rate.
lockIn: Fixed certificate tenor; encashment before maturity is restricted
minimumInvestment: Scheme minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Accrued interest is taxable at slab rates each year even though no cash is received; under the old regime the accrual is treated as reinvested for the deduction framework, which partially offsets the tax. The scheme is not exempt despite often being described as tax-saving.
fees: No entry cost; premature encashment conditions are set by the scheme.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals and specified categories permitted by the scheme; NRIs are generally not eligible.
risks: Annual accrual tax creates a cash-flow cost before maturity
The rate resets at each new certificate issue
Long tenor locks the money with limited premature encashment
Real return can be negative for higher-slab investors
suitability: A modest, sovereign-backed fixed-income holding for an old-regime taxpayer who values certainty and can hold to maturity. Not attractive to an investor whose other taxable options already cover the same need.
commonMistakes: Believing the certificate is tax-free
Forgetting the annual interest accrual for tax purposes
Buying it purely for the deduction without comparing alternatives

name: Kisan Vikas Patra
oneLiner: A post-office certificate that doubles the invested amount over a period fixed by the government, with no income-tax deduction benefit.
returnMechanism: The certificate accrues a declared rate until the amount doubles; the doubling period is notified by the government and is adjusted when the rate changes. The return is entirely administrative interest with no market linkage.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically; the headline term is the doubling period, which changes when the notified rate changes. Any quoted figure is a point-in-time fact.
maxDrawdownNote: No nominal drawdown; the notified doubling period can be lengthened for new issues, which reduces the effective rate for later investors.
lockIn: Fixed certificate tenor; premature encashment is restricted and permitted only on the scheme's conditions after a minimum period
minimumInvestment: Scheme minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Interest is fully taxable at slab rates, accruing over the tenor; the scheme carries no deduction for contributions. Because no cash is received until maturity, the annual accrual can create a tax liability in advance of cash.
fees: No entry cost; early encashment rules are scheme-specific.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals and specified categories permitted by the scheme; NRIs are generally not eligible.
risks: Fully taxable interest with no deduction benefit
Long lock-up to reach the doubling point
Effective rate falls when the government lengthens the doubling period for new issues
Liquidity before maturity is limited
suitability: A simple sovereign-credit savings option for an investor who wants a target-driven, no-market-risk commitment and is comfortable with the tax drag. Not a tax-saving instrument.
commonMistakes: Buying KVP for a tax deduction it does not provide
Ignoring the accrual tax in the cash-flow plan
Not checking the current doubling period before purchase

name: Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme
oneLiner: A government savings scheme for investors above the specified age that pays quarterly interest at an administratively set rate on a capped deposit.
returnMechanism: The government pays a declared rate, reset periodically, on the deposited amount, with interest paid out quarterly rather than compounded. The return is entirely administrative interest; there is no market linkage.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically, typically pitched above ordinary small-savings rates because the scheme is designed for retirement income. The quarterly payout means no compounding within the account.
lockIn: A fixed initial tenor with the option to extend, subject to the scheme's conditions
minimumInvestment: A small minimum deposit with a statutory maximum per account
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates; a senior citizen can claim a limited deduction for deposit interest under the old regime, which the new regime does not provide. TDS applies above the applicable threshold, which is higher for senior citizens.
fees: No entry cost; premature closure is permitted only on the scheme's conditions and involves a rate adjustment.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals above the scheme's age threshold, with different eligibility for those who retired on superannuation or under a voluntary retirement scheme within the specified window.
risks: Interest is paid out and is fully taxable, so the real income falls if inflation rises
Rates reset at each new issue and on extension
The deposit cap limits the amount of retirement capital that can be parked here
Premature exit is restricted
suitability: A sovereign-backed income sleeve for a retiree who wants predictable quarterly cash flow and can accept the tax drag. It does not address inflation over a long retirement, so it needs equity or inflation-sensitive assets alongside it.
commonMistakes: Placing the entire retirement corpus in the scheme and ignoring inflation
Assuming the quarterly payout is tax-free
Overlooking the deposit cap and the extension conditions
Failing to compare the post-tax payout with other income options

name: Post Office Monthly Income Scheme
oneLiner: A post-office deposit that pays a monthly interest amount at an administratively set rate on a capped balance, designed for regular income rather than growth.
returnMechanism: The government pays a declared rate as monthly interest, with principal returned at maturity. The return is entirely administrative interest; there is no market participation and no equity upside.
expectedReturn: Administratively set and reset periodically; the payout is monthly and does not compound within the account, so the effective annual return is simply the declared rate on the deposited amount.
lockIn: A fixed tenor; premature closure is permitted on the scheme's conditions, with a rate adjustment in some cases
minimumInvestment: A small minimum deposit with a statutory maximum per account
taxTreatment: Monthly interest is taxable at slab rates as it is received, with TDS above the applicable threshold. The scheme does not provide an income-tax deduction.
fees: No entry cost; premature closure conditions are set by the scheme.
investorEligibility: Resident individuals, with joint-account rules and stated maximum limits; NRIs are generally not eligible.
risks: No compounding: interest is paid out and must be reinvested manually to grow
Taxed at slab rates as received
Rates reset at each new issue
Fixed nominal payout loses purchasing power over a long tenor
suitability: A simple monthly-income option for a conservative investor, on the understanding that the payout is fixed in nominal terms and fully taxable. Not suitable as the only retirement-income source over a long horizon.
commonMistakes: Spending the monthly interest without a reinvestment plan
Assuming the payout rises with inflation
Ignoring the deposit cap when planning the monthly income

name: RBI Floating Rate Savings Bond
oneLiner: A government savings bond whose coupon floats with the prevailing National Savings Certificate rate, with a long lock-up and restricted early exit.
returnMechanism: The bond pays a coupon set at a fixed spread over the prevailing NSC rate, reset periodically. The return is therefore administrative interest that follows the small-savings rate rather than a market index; it is not inflation-linked despite the floating-coupon label.
expectedReturn: A rate linked to the NSC rate at each reset; the mechanism can be described, but the level is not forecastable and is reset administratively. Whether a tranche is open for subscription is time-sensitive and must be verified.
lockIn: A long fixed tenor, with early exit permitted only on the specified conditions for defined investor categories
minimumInvestment: A small minimum subscription per the issue terms; verify the current offering
taxTreatment: Interest is fully taxable at slab rates and is paid on the specified schedule, with TDS above the threshold. The bond carries no capital-gains concession, and the floating coupon does not change the tax character of the interest.
fees: No entry cost or expense ratio; the practical cost is the illiquidity of a long tenor with narrow exit windows.
investorEligibility: Individuals and specified categories per the issue terms, with different early-exit rights for senior citizens; whether a tranche is currently on offer must be checked before planning around it.
risks: The floating coupon can fall when small-savings rates are cut, reducing future income
A long lock-up with very limited early exit
Issuance windows are not continuous, so the bond may not be available when needed
Fully taxable interest with no compounding within the bond
suitability: For conservative investors who want sovereign credit and a coupon that adjusts with the small-savings cycle, and who will not need the money during the lock-up. Not a substitute for a liquid allocation, and not an inflation hedge.
commonMistakes: Mistaking the floating coupon for inflation protection
Buying without checking the reset benchmark and the current availability
Planning liquidity around an early-exit option that may not apply

name: Liquid fund
oneLiner: An open-ended debt mutual fund that holds very short-maturity, high-quality money-market instruments to give near-cash access with a small yield over a savings account.
returnMechanism: The fund earns accrual on short-dated instruments plus small price changes as securities roll down the curve. The return is interest-driven with minimal duration; there is no equity participation.
expectedReturn: Close to short money-market rates, net of a small expense ratio. Rates track the policy-rate cycle, so the return changes with the environment rather than being fixed.
historicalReturnNote: Liquid funds have generally delivered stable, low-volatility accrual returns with rare, brief disruptions in stressed markets; they have also seen isolated mark-to-market shocks when a held issuer's paper repriced.
maxDrawdownNote: Normally a fraction of a percentage; in stressed credit markets a single downgrade has produced unusually sharp but rare one-day declines.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates with the gain deemed short-term regardless of holding period, so the return is taxed as ordinary income. Withdrawals also carry a graded exit-load structure in many schemes, which is a cost rather than a tax.
fees: A small expense ratio is deducted daily from net asset value; some schemes charge a graded exit load for very short holding periods. Direct plans cost less than regular plans.
investorEligibility: Any investor who completes the fund's KYC; NRIs subject to the fund's conditions for repatriation.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Liquid-fund yields follow the policy-rate cycle; replace with the prevailing money-market level.

risks: Credit events in held paper can cause unexpected mark-to-market loss
Exit loads penalise very short holding periods
Returns are fully taxable at slab, so the post-tax pickup over a savings account can be small
Yield falls when rates fall
suitability: A cash-management tool for emergency reserves and money parked for weeks, where same-day or next-day access matters more than return. Not a place for long-horizon money that needs growth.
commonMistakes: Treating a liquid fund as a fixed deposit and ignoring the small possibility of a credit shock
Holding for a few days and absorbing exit loads
Using it for a goal more than a year away
Comparing pre-tax returns without adjusting for the slab-rate tax

name: Ultra-short duration debt fund
oneLiner: A debt fund holding short-dated paper with a slightly longer duration than a liquid fund, aimed at a modestly higher yield for money parked over weeks to a few months.
returnMechanism: The fund earns interest accrual on short-maturity corporate and money-market paper with a small amount of duration-driven price movement. Return is interest plus a small mark-to-market component.
expectedReturn: Broadly the short-end market rate plus a small credit and duration spread, net of expenses; the level moves with the policy-rate cycle.
maxDrawdownNote: Small; a credit downgrade or a sharp rate move can produce a temporary loss larger than a liquid fund's.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates with the gain deemed short-term regardless of holding period; pre-2023 units retain the older treatment.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans cheaper than regular. Exit loads are less common than in liquid funds but scheme-specific.
investorEligibility: Any investor who completes KYC; scheme documents set the permitted maturity profile.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast; assumes a steady rate environment. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Credit risk in the corporate paper sleeve
Duration loss if short rates rise sharply
Slab-rate taxation erodes the pickup over a liquid fund
Chasing yield by moving down the credit curve
suitability: One step out from a liquid fund for money that can stay parked for a few months. Not a substitute for a short-duration allocation for multi-year money.
commonMistakes: Choosing the highest-yielding scheme in the category without checking its credit profile
Assuming the category is risk-free
Ignoring the tax drag at higher slabs

name: Money market fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that invests only in money-market instruments up to one year, distinguished by instrument eligibility rather than merely by duration.
returnMechanism: The fund earns the prevailing money-market yield on treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit, with minimal duration. The return is interest accrual, not capital appreciation.
expectedReturn: Money-market rates net of a small expense ratio; closely tracks the policy-rate cycle and changes as that cycle changes.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Acquired on or after 1 April 2023, gains are taxed at slab rates as deemed short-term regardless of holding period.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans cost less. Exit loads are uncommon in this category but must be checked per scheme.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; the regulatory definition restricts the fund's holdings to money-market instruments.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast; follows money-market rates, which are not stable. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Commercial-paper credit risk, though typically short-dated and high-rated
Rate resets reduce yield quickly when the policy rate falls
Slab-rate taxation
Category definition does not guarantee quality of every holding
suitability: A precise short-term parking vehicle where the investor wants the strict money-market mandate. Not a long-term compounding asset.
commonMistakes: Confusing money-market funds with liquid funds and assuming identical mandates
Ignoring the tax rate at higher slabs
Expecting a stable yield across the rate cycle

name: Short duration debt fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that holds a portfolio with a short but not minimal duration, targeting a modestly higher yield for money that can stay invested for a few years.
returnMechanism: The return combines coupon accrual on high-quality corporate and government paper with price movement as the portfolio's duration reacts to rate changes. Interest dominates, but rate moves can add or subtract meaningfully.
expectedReturn: Driven by the short-to-medium segment of the yield curve, net of expenses; the return is market-determined and changes with the rate cycle.
historicalReturnNote: Short-duration funds have generally shown small drawdowns over rolling periods, with losses concentrated in sharp rate-rise episodes.
maxDrawdownNote: A meaningful rise in yields can produce a loss over weeks to months; the short duration limits its size relative to longer funds.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates as deemed short-term regardless of holding period, so the fund is not a capital-gains vehicle.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans cost less than regular. Exit loads are scheme-specific.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; the scheme's mandate sets the permitted duration band.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Replace with your own rate and credit assumptions.

risks: Duration loss in a rate-rise cycle
Credit migration in the corporate sleeve
Slab-rate taxation on all post-March-2023 acquisitions
Complacency in a category usually described as low-risk
suitability: A core debt allocation for goals two to three years out, where the investor wants a small yield pickup over deposits and accepts small interim losses. Not for money needed at short notice.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'short' means no price movement
Holding for less than a year and being surprised by a loss
Chasing category-toppers without reading the credit profile
Forgetting that all post-2023 gains are taxed at slab

name: Corporate bond fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that must hold a high proportion of corporate bonds, typically AA+ and above, aiming for a credit spread over government securities.
returnMechanism: The return is the coupon accrual on high-grade corporate paper plus the spread over government securities, adjusted for price changes as rates and credit spreads move. The spread is compensation for corporate credit risk.
expectedReturn: Government-securities yield plus a corporate spread, net of expenses. Both components move with the market; nothing is contractually fixed for the unit holder.
maxDrawdownNote: Rate rises and spread widening can produce losses; high-grade portfolios recover as bonds mature but the interim mark is real for a seller.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Post-March-2023 acquisitions are taxed at slab rates with gains deemed short-term regardless of holding period; pre-2023 units keep the older capital-gains framework.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans lower than regular. Exit loads are scheme-specific.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; the SEBI mandate requires a minimum corporate-bond allocation and an investment-grade universe.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Spreads and rates change; replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Spread widening produces mark-to-market losses
Credit event in a large holding
Slab-rate tax treatment limits the net pickup
Liquidity in the underlying bonds may be thinner than the fund's own redemption terms suggest
suitability: A medium-term debt holding for investors who want a structured, diversified credit exposure above government securities. Not for near-term money or for an investor unwilling to see interim losses.
commonMistakes: Comparing the fund's recent return with a fixed deposit without adjusting for risk and tax
Ignoring the mandate's minimum corporate allocation when assessing risk
Selling after a mark-to-market fall and locking in the loss

name: Banking and PSU debt fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that must hold a high share of bonds issued by banks, public-sector undertakings and similar entities, giving a concentrated but typically high-grade credit exposure.
returnMechanism: Return is coupon accrual on bank and PSU paper plus rate-driven price changes. The spread over government securities is modest because the issuers are typically highly rated and in some cases implicitly supported.
expectedReturn: Close to the high-grade corporate segment of the curve, net of expenses; sensitive to the rate cycle.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Gains on units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates and deemed short-term regardless of holding period.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans lower. Exit loads scheme-specific.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; the mandate restricts the issuer universe to banks, PSUs and similar entities.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Replace with your own rate assumptions.

risks: Concentration in a single issuer segment
Duration loss in rate-rise cycles
Implicit-support assumptions are a marketing argument, not a contractual guarantee
Slab-rate taxation
suitability: A debt holding for investors who want high-grade exposure without the effort of picking issuers. It is a segment bet, so it should sit alongside, not replace, a broader debt allocation.
commonMistakes: Assuming PSU exposure is risk-free
Ignoring duration when comparing schemes in the category
Treating the mandate as a guarantee of issuer quality

name: Gilt fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that invests only in government securities with no corporate credit exposure, taking pure interest rate risk across a range of maturities.
returnMechanism: The return is the sovereign coupon plus or minus price changes as yields move. With no credit risk, the entire variation in return comes from duration and from the shape of the yield curve.
expectedReturn: The government-securities yield for the portfolio's average maturity, net of expenses; the return can be significantly above or below that level in any single year because of price moves.
historicalReturnNote: Gilt funds have delivered strong years when yields fell and drawdowns when yields rose, illustrating that sovereign credit removes default risk but not market risk.
maxDrawdownNote: Falls materially when yields rise, more than short-duration funds and proportionately to average maturity.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Gains on units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates and deemed short-term regardless of holding period; pre-2023 units retain the older treatment.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; index-style gilt funds cost less than actively managed ones. Direct plans cheaper than regular.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; the mandate restricts holdings to government securities.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Gilt fund returns depend heavily on the rate path; replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Duration risk, which is the dominant source of loss
Rate cycle timing: buying after a rally leaves capital loss risk
Slab-rate taxation
Investors often mistake sovereign credit for capital safety
suitability: A high-quality duration tool for investors who want to express a view on rates or match a long-dated liability. Not a substitute for a short-duration allocation for near-term money.
commonMistakes: Buying gilt funds for 'safety' without understanding duration
Extrapolating a rally year into the future
Holding for a few months and selling into a rate rise

name: Gilt fund with constant duration
oneLiner: A gilt fund whose mandate keeps the portfolio's duration within a tight band, typically targeting a specified target maturity such as ten years.
returnMechanism: The fund maintains a roughly constant duration by rolling holdings, so the return is a continuous exposure to a specific point on the yield curve rather than a declining duration as bonds mature. Return is coupon plus rate-driven price change.
expectedReturn: Closely tracks the yield at the targeted maturity plus the effect of rate moves. Because duration is held constant, the fund does not naturally de-risk as time passes, unlike a target-maturity product.
maxDrawdownNote: Meaningful losses when long yields rise; the constant duration means the fund keeps taking the same rate risk rather than shortening over time.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Gains on units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates and deemed short-term regardless of holding period.
fees: Small daily expense ratio; direct plans cheaper.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast; the value depends on the target duration and the rate path. Replace with your own assumptions.

risks: The constant duration means no natural de-risking as the holding period shortens
Large mark-to-market losses in a sustained rate-rise cycle
Category is small, so scheme choice is limited
Slab-rate taxation of gains
suitability: For an investor who wants a long-bond exposure held as a strategic allocation rather than a liability-matching maturity. Not for money that must be available intact at a near date.
commonMistakes: Confusing constant duration with target maturity
Assuming the fund's duration falls as the goal approaches
Buying after a fall in yields without checking the embedded yield

name: Target maturity debt fund
oneLiner: An open-ended debt fund or ETF with a defined maturity date, holding bonds that mature around that date so the portfolio's duration declines mechanically toward zero.
returnMechanism: The fund buys bonds maturing near the target date and holds them largely to maturity. Return comes from the initial yield locked at purchase plus reinvestment of interim coupons at whatever rates prevail; as maturity approaches, price sensitivity falls.
expectedReturn: Largely determined by the yield at the time of purchase and the target maturity chosen, subject to reinvestment risk on interim cash flows. This is a structural feature, not a promise of a fixed return.
historicalReturnNote: Target-maturity products have behaved close to the underlying bond yields when held to maturity, with interim marks moving with rates.
maxDrawdownNote: Interim net asset value can fall when yields rise, but the mechanical shortening of duration pulls the price toward par as maturity approaches.
lockIn: None, but the structure is designed to be held to the target date; early exit occurs at the market price
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Gains on units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates as deemed short-term regardless of holding period. The fund's taxable event for the investor remains the redemption or sale, not the bond maturity inside the fund.
fees: Low expense ratios, particularly for the ETF versions; direct plans cheaper.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor; ETFs also require a demat account and exchange access.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. The actual outcome depends on the yield at purchase and reinvestment rates; replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Reinvestment risk on interim coupons
Credit risk if the mandate includes non-sovereign issuers
Slab-rate taxation reduces the net outcome
Investors may sell early at a mark-to-market loss if they need money before the target date
suitability: A liability-matching tool for a known, dated goal where the investor wants yield visibility and automatic duration reduction. Not for an investor who may need the money before the target date.
commonMistakes: Treating the target maturity like a guaranteed-return product
Selling early into a rate rise
Ignoring the credit quality of the underlying index
Assuming tax parity with a bond held directly

name: Debt exchange-traded fund
oneLiner: A debt portfolio that trades on an exchange like a stock, offering low-cost access to government or high-grade bond indices but with a market price that can diverge from net asset value.
returnMechanism: Return is the underlying portfolio's accrual and price change, less a low expense ratio. The exchange price is a market price, so realised returns depend on the execution price as well as the portfolio.
expectedReturn: Close to the underlying bond index yield, net of a very low expense ratio; execution slippage and the spread at entry and exit modify the realised outcome.
maxDrawdownNote: NAV moves with rates; the traded price can diverge from NAV in stressed or thin markets, producing a loss beyond the portfolio's own move.
minimumInvestment: One unit plus brokerage, so the ticket can be small
taxTreatment: Units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates with the gain deemed short-term regardless of holding period. Exchange transactions also carry securities transaction tax and stamp duty as applicable to the instrument.
fees: Very low expense ratio, often the lowest in the debt category; brokerage, exchange charges and the bid-ask spread are added on top at execution.
investorEligibility: Any investor with a demat and trading account; institutional creation and redemption keeps the price anchored in normal conditions.
risks: Price can trade at a premium or discount to net asset value when liquidity is thin
Low on-screen volumes can make exit expensive for larger orders
Slab-rate taxation
Rate-driven NAV falls when yields rise
suitability: A low-cost way to hold a debt index for investors who execute carefully with limit orders. Not suitable for large lump-sum exits in illiquid periods without checking the order book.
commonMistakes: Using market orders in thin books and paying a wide spread
Assuming the traded price always equals net asset value
Choosing a debt ETF for very short holding periods without counting the cost

name: Credit risk fund
oneLiner: A debt fund that must hold the majority of its portfolio in lower-rated corporate bonds, earning a credit spread in exchange for accepting real default risk.
returnMechanism: The return is the coupon on below-top-rated paper plus spread changes, less actual credit losses. The spread is the market's payment for taking issuers whose ratings are lower and whose access to refinancing is weaker.
expectedReturn: A visible spread over high-grade debt, part of which is expected to be lost to defaults and downgrades over time. The gross spread is not the net return.
historicalReturnNote: This category has suffered well-publicised credit events in the Indian market, with side-pocketing and prolonged NAV marks; the category's realised dispersion between schemes is wider than its averages suggest.
maxDrawdownNote: A single large downgrade or default can produce NAV losses far outside the category's normal range and can be difficult to recover.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Gains on units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates deemed short-term; a loss may be set off against other capital gains subject to the rules.
fees: Expense ratios are higher than in high-grade categories and are a drag on an already risk-priced return; direct plans cheaper than regular.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor, but the category requires the investor to read credit quality rather than assume it.

illustrativeMetrics.note: Illustrative modelling input only, not a forecast. Defaults are lumpy and not captured by a smooth volatility figure; replace with your own assumptions.

risks: Default or downgrade of a large holding
Concentration in a small number of issuers
Refinancing stress in a tight-liquidity environment
Losses can be illiquid and slow to resolve
suitability: Only for investors who can read a portfolio's credit holdings, can tolerate lumpy losses and are not relying on the money at a specific date. Not a substitute for a high-grade debt allocation.
commonMistakes: Buying the category's highest trailing yield without reading the underlying issuers
Assuming a diversified fund removes issuer concentration
Treating a single year's spread income as a sustainable return
Overlooking side-pocketing mechanics before investing

name: Dynamic bond fund
oneLiner: A debt fund whose manager can move duration anywhere on the curve, making the interest-rate exposure an active decision rather than a fixed mandate.
returnMechanism: The return is accrual on the held bonds plus the price impact of the duration position taken. Because duration can change materially, the fund's return resembles a rate view more than a fixed-income steady accrual.
expectedReturn: Driven by the manager's duration calls and the rate environment; a wide range of outcomes is possible and no level is contractual.
historicalReturnNote: Dynamic bond funds have produced strong years in rate-cutting cycles and losses in rate-rise cycles, with manager dispersion wider than in mandated-duration categories.
maxDrawdownNote: Can be substantial when the manager is positioned for falling rates and rates rise instead.
minimumInvestment: Scheme-specific minimum, typically small
taxTreatment: Units acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are taxed at slab rates with the gain deemed short-term regardless of holding period.
fees: Expense ratios reflect active management and are higher than index-style debt products; direct plans cheaper.
investorEligibility: Any KYC-compliant investor.
risks: Rate-call risk concentrated in one manager
Style drift across managers under the same label
Slab-rate taxation
Investors buy after a good year and sit through the bad one
suitability: For an investor who wants active rate management within a debt allocation and can tolerate interim losses. Not for an investor who wants a predictable accrual or who cannot assess the manager's duration positioning.
commonMistakes: Choosing a dynamic bond fund based on a one-year return
Assuming the category means steady income
Ignoring the disclosed portfolio duration before investing
Using it as a short-term parking place

name: Listed non-convertible debenture
oneLiner: A corporate bond listed on an exchange that pays a stated interest rate and repays principal on a set date, with credit risk belonging to the issuer.
returnMechanism: The investor receives the contractual coupon and principal repayment; the return above a government bond of the same maturity is the credit spread, which is the price of the issuer's default risk and the bond's illiquidity. Secondary-market price moves add or subtract capital gains.
expectedReturn: The yield at which the bond is bought. Public issues often carry coupons above bank deposit rates, but the excess is compensation for issuer credit risk and thin secondary liquidity, not a free premium.
historicalReturnNote: Most investment-grade NCDs pay as contracted; the segment's history includes defaults in lower-rated issuers and, in a few cases, prolonged resolution with recovery below par.
maxDrawdownNote: Prices fall when yields rise or when the issuer's perceived credit quality deteriorates; a default can permanently impair principal.
minimumInvestment: Public issues set small face-value lots; secondary-market lots are larger and must be checked before assuming access
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates as it accrues or is received, with tax deducted at source above the applicable threshold. Capital gains on listed bonds held beyond the long-term threshold are taxed without indexation, while short-term gains are taxed at slab. Unlisted bonds and debentures acquired on or after 1 April 2023 face a deemed short-term treatment regardless of holding period, so listing status matters.
fees: No fund expense ratio; the costs are the bid-ask spread, brokerage and stamp duty on the exchange trade. Thin trading in many scrips makes the spread the main cost.
investorEligibility: Any investor with a demat and trading account for exchange trades; public issues set their own minimum lots and categories.
risks: Issuer default or restructuring
Thin secondary liquidity makes an early exit expensive
Interest rate risk if yields rise
Concentration: a single bond is one company's credit
suitability: For investors who can read a credit profile and want a defined maturity and coupon, holding to maturity rather than trading. Not suitable as a substitute for a diversified debt fund or for money needed at short notice.
commonMistakes: Buying on yield alone without reading the rating rationale
Assuming exchange listing implies an active market
Ignoring the subordination and covenant terms in the issue document
Treating a high coupon as evidence of safety

name: Unlisted NCD or privately placed bond
oneLiner: A corporate bond issued by private placement and not traded on an exchange, bought directly or through a distributor and typically held to maturity.
returnMechanism: The return is the contractual coupon plus any discount to face at purchase. Without an exchange price, the value of the contract is only the issuer's promise; the spread over listed paper compensates for illiquidity and weaker disclosure.
expectedReturn: The negotiated yield, usually above comparable listed bonds. The premium is the price of illiquidity and reduced information; it is not a free gain.
maxDrawdownNote: No market price moves daily, but credit deterioration, missed payments or restructuring can impair principal without any quoted price change.
minimumInvestment: Placement minimums are set by the issuer and are often large; retail access depends on the specific issue
taxTreatment: Interest is taxable at slab rates, with tax deducted at source where applicable. Unlisted bonds and debentures acquired on or after 1 April 2023 are deemed short-term capital assets regardless of holding period, so gains are taxed at slab with no indexation; pre-2023 holdings keep the older framework.
fees: No exchange or fund costs; distributor commission is often embedded in the issue economics. There is no reliable market to exit at a fair price.
investorEligibility: Placement eligibility and minimum sizes are issuer- and issue-specific; many are privately negotiated and effectively institutional.
risks: Very limited public disclosure and no market price
Illiquidity: no realistic exit before maturity
Credit deterioration is hard to detect from outside
Documentation and enforcement are weaker than in exchange-listed instruments
suitability: Only for an investor who has done genuine credit work, is comfortable holding to maturity and can absorb a loss without liquidity needs. Not for retail portfolios that rely on valuation or exit options.
commonMistakes: Assuming the higher coupon is compensation for liquidity alone rather than for real default risk
Relying on a distributor's summary instead of the offering document
